newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban say demilitarisation of Kabul unacceptable.
newsitem.headline: Taleban say demilitarisation of Kabul unacceptable.

text.p: Afghanistan's purist Islamic Taleban movement said on Wednesday a demand by its foes that Kabul be demilitarised as a condition for a ceasefire was unacceptable.
"He has set forth an unacceptable condition for a ceasefire, the demilitarisation of Kabul, which is not practical," Acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told a news conference.

Mutaqi was referring to northern Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum, who has been negotiating on a ceasefire on behalf of a tripartite alliance of Taleban foes which includes ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.
The demilitarisation demand was first voiced by Masood, military chief in the ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani, and endorsed by the anti-Taleban alliance on Tuesday.
"We want a ceasefire on conditions of (an) exchange of prisoners followed by talks," Mutaqi said.
Pakistani Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar, who has been trying to broker a truce, said in Islamabad on Tuesday he was hopeful a ceasefire in fighting north of Kabul could be agreed.
Later, the United Nations Security Council unanimously agreed on a call for a ceasefire and political negotiations.

Mutaqi said talks were still going on with Dostum, who sent tanks, artillery and men to join Masood's front-line, but suggested the discussions would end if the Uzbeks joined the attacks on the Taleban.
Masood spokesmen said Dostum's artillery helped Masood take Bagram airbase, 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul, last week and in an attack a little closer to the capital on Wednesday.
Taleban fighters on the front-line say they have no evidence of the Uzbeks being involved in the fighting and Mutaqi echoed that view.
"So far, it is not clear whether Dostum forces are involved or not," he said.
"We do not have any problem with him. If he wants to create any, it belongs to him. If any side attacks, that side will be our enemy," he added.
The Taleban have not been recognised abroad as the new Afghan government and have been widely criticised in the west for barring women from work and school.
They say ways around the problem of separating men and women in education and the workplace could be worked out when Afghanistan is at peace.
That still appears a long way off and Mutaqi said the Taleban would give up neither territory nor Islam's stern Sharia law they have imposed on the three-quarters of Afghanistan they now control.

"I can tell you once again with confidence that the ominous plans of our enemies will never succeed in Afghanistan. We will defend areas under our control until the last drop of blood and with our last Taleb," he said.
"We will never bow to any military or political pressure in the areas where we have implemented Islamic Sharia.
